priority: HIGH — matched to all 7 users, deadline 70 days out, and it is Finding 1's pay-at-submission pattern sitting in the COMPETITION category

what_it_actually_is_verbatim: 'The only quarterly journal in the world to publish the academic research papers of secondary students.'
taxonomy_note: This is a PUBLICATION VENUE — the same thing as the six rows I flagged in `research` (CR1-010…018) — but it sits in `competition`, presumably because of the Emerson Prize attached to it. So the publication-venue taxonomy gap is not confined to one category. Whatever is decided for the journals must cover this row too, or the corpus will treat identical objects differently based on which category someone happened to file them under.
fee_verbatim: 'Each essay must be accompanied by a $70 submission fee'
fee_timing_note: Collected during account setup by invoice or card — i.e. paid up front, before any editorial decision. The page does NOT say when exactly, and does NOT state whether it is refundable if the paper is not published.
ACCEPTANCE_RATE_OFFICIAL: 'We publish about 5% of the essays we receive.'
the_arithmetic: $70 at submission against an officially published ~5% acceptance rate. Naively that is ~$1,400 per publication — a WORSE expected cost than JRHS's ~$1,167 (CR1-010), which was the row I flagged as the corpus's biggest financial risk. BUT two things cut the other way and must be stated with it: (a) 'Essays are eligible for the next three issues', so one $70 fee buys three consecutive chances rather than one; (b) unlike the pay-to-publish journals, a 5% rate means TCR is genuinely, severely selective, and publication there is a real distinction rather than a purchased byline. The honest summary is: same fee STRUCTURE as JRHS, opposite prestige PROFILE.
why_that_distinction_is_the_whole_point: This is the case that shows why 'paid = bad' is the wrong rule. JRHS charges $350 at submission for a ~30% shot at a venue with no external standing. TCR charges $70 at submission for a ~5% shot at the most respected secondary-school history journal in existence. A gate keyed on cost alone ranks JRHS as five times worse; a student's actual expected value runs the other way.
eligibility_verbatim: 'You may submit a history research paper to The Concord Review if you completed the paper before finishing secondary school and you have not yet enrolled in a college or university.' country_note: An explicit, unambiguous worldwide-inclusive eligibility statement sitting in the eligibility section — the strongest placement. Home-schooled students named explicitly. The row currently stores NO countries at all.
sole_author_note: 'You must be the sole author' — no team submissions. Also in English only, which is the same capability gate flagged for Breakthrough Junior Challenge (CR1-130).
deadlines_all_verbatim: Summer issue: February 1, 11:59pm EST. Fall issue: May 1, 11:59pm EDT. Winter issue: August 1, 11:59pm EDT. Spring issue: November 1, 11:59pm EST.
deadline_note: FOUR deadlines per year, one per quarterly issue. The stored 2026-11-01 is the SPRING issue deadline and is correct — 70 days out. But storing only one of four means a student who misses it is told nothing about the next (2027-02-01). This row genuinely needs a recurring-deadline representation, not a single date.
emerson_prize: Awarded annually to students published in TCR during the previous academic year 'who have shown outstanding promise in history at the high school level'. Over 200 students have won since 1995; recent recipients received $1,000. NOTE: the prize is downstream of publication — you cannot enter the Emerson Prize, you become eligible by being published.

recommendation: Enrich with the worldwide eligibility, the sole-author and English rules, the 5% rate, and all four quarterly deadlines. And show the fee and the acceptance rate TOGETHER — $70 alone reads as cheap, 5% alone reads as prestigious, and only the pair is honest.

priority: HIGH — Europe's flagship research competition, in the corpus with no deadline, no countries and no entry mechanism
live_opportunity_title: European Union Contest for Young Scientists (EUCYS)
organization: European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation
stored_state: cycle_status=upcoming, deadline=NULL, min_age=14, max_age=20, cost=0.00, NO countries, NO entry mechanism
age_note: Stored 14-20 is CORRECT — one of the few rows whose age data already matches the source. Note it starts at 14, the very bottom of ORYN's band.
entry_mechanism_verbatim: 'organisers of participating National Contests are invited to nominate the first prize winning teams from the national contest to EUCYS'; participants are 'young European scientists aged between 14 and 20, who have won first prize at their national science competition'
entry_note: You cannot apply to EUCYS. You must WIN FIRST PRIZE at your national science competition and be nominated. That is a materially higher bar than 'do well nationally' — second place nationally is not enough. The stored row says nothing about any of this.
next_edition_note: That is 30 days from retrieval — but it is the EVENT, not a deadline. There is no student-facing EUCYS deadline; nomination happens through the national contest months earlier. Storing 2026-09-22 as a deadline would repeat exactly the Purple Comet error (CR1-137).
team_rule_verbatim: 'Projects can be composed by individuals or teams of up to 3 participants'
prizes: Four 1st prizes at €7,000; four 2nd at €5,000; four 3rd at €3,500; Special Jury Prize €2,500; plus donated and honorary prizes (including SIYSS and LIYSF places).
scale: 'from almost 40 countries' at EUCYS 2026; scope described as 'EU members and Associated and Neighbourhood Countries'.
TURKIYE_PARTICIPATION_CONFIRMED: YES. The European Commission's own news pages record Türkiye winning at EUCYS: at the 36th edition (2025, Riga) second and third prizes 'went to projects from Türkiye, Portugal, Greece, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Hungary and the USA'; Turkey also appears among prize-winners at the 32nd edition. So Türkiye is a participating country in practice, evidenced by the organiser itself.
THE_CHAIN_THIS_LIKELY_COMPLETES: This is probably the missing piece of TÜBİTAK 2204-A §7.1.2 (CR1-002). Established: (a) EUCYS entry is by nomination of national-contest FIRST PRIZE winners; (b) Türkiye participates and wins, per the Commission; (c) TÜBİTAK 2204-A is Türkiye's national high-school research project competition, and TÜBİTAK's own call document says it sends winners to 'Uluslararası Proje Yarışmaları' where a top-three placing triggers **sınavsız yerleştirme** — exam-free university placement.
WHAT_I_HAVE_NOT_PROVEN: Neither side names the other. The Commission does not identify TÜBİTAK as Türkiye's national contest organiser, and TÜBİTAK's call never names EUCYS. The join is highly probable — there is no other obvious candidate for Türkiye's national science competition at this level — but it remains an INFERENCE, and it sits underneath a claim about university admission rights. **Do not tell a Turkish student that winning 2204-A leads to EUCYS and thence to exam-free placement until one of the two organisations states the link.** This is precisely the kind of chain where a plausible join becomes a promise, and the stakes here are a student's university place.
how_to_close_it: Either (a) TÜBİTAK publishes which international competitions it sends 2204-A winners to, or (b) the EUCYS participating-national-contests list names the Turkish organiser. One page from either side settles it.
cost_note: Stored 0.00; no fee stated on the official page either way. Given entry is by nomination rather than application, a student fee is structurally unlikely — but 'unlikely' is not 'verified', and per the founder's cost rule this should arguably be NULL until stated.
eligible_countries: Nomination via participating National Contests — 'almost 40 countries', described as EU members plus Associated and Neighbourhood Countries. Türkiye confirmed present. No official list retrieved.
confidence_caveat: High for everything except the TÜBİTAK↔EUCYS join, which is explicitly marked unproven above.

priority: URGENT — 19 days out, matched to all 7 users, and the row does not say a student needs a TEAM and a TEACHER to enter
live_opportunity_title: Wharton Global High School Investment Competition
organization: University of Pennsylvania — Wharton School (Wharton Global Youth Program)
stored_state: cycle_status=open, deadline=2026-09-11, cost=0.00, eligible_grades=4 values, NO countries, NO team/advisor requirement
deadline_verbatim: 'September 11' — 'Registration closes; all student team account must be created (5:00 p.m. ET)' for the 2026-2027 competition year
deadline_note: NINETEEN DAYS from retrieval. Stored deadline is CORRECT — this row's problem is not the date.
THE_GAP_THAT_MATTERS: Entry requires a TEAM OF FOUR TO SIX plus a TEACHER FROM THE STUDENT'S SCHOOL as advisor. Verbatim: 'Students work in teams of four to six, guided by a teacher from their school as their advisor.' The stored row records none of this. So ORYN can show a lone student a 19-day countdown to something they cannot enter alone — they must recruit three to five classmates AND persuade a teacher, inside 19 days. That is a materially different ask from 'apply', and the lead time is exactly what makes it urgent to say now rather than later.
eligible_countries: NOT STATED. The page cites participation statistics from multiple countries but carries no eligibility-by-country rule. Per the placement test a participation statistic is not an eligibility statement — the same call I made for The Earth Prize's '169 countries' and Blue Ocean's '173 countries'. Left unset.
what_teams_do: Develop 'a long-term investment strategy' around a case study of a Wharton alumnus; research 'financial markets, industries, companies, and investment opportunities'; produce an Investment Policy Statement and a Comprehensive Final Report; and manage a virtual portfolio through the Wharton Investment Simulator.
commitment_profile: NOT a single-submission competition. Timeline: begins 2026-09-28; deliverables due 2026-10-09, 2026-11-06 and 2026-12-04; virtual semifinals; Global Finale 2027-04-29/30. That is a **multi-month team commitment running from September to April** — directly relevant to ORYN's time-budget logic (AGENTS.md §64) and completely invisible in a row that stores one date.
why_it_fills_a_measured_gap: CR1-152 measured Business at 5 and Economics at 2. This is a serious, free, team-based finance competition from a top business school — and it is one of the few in the corpus with a genuine multi-month research arc rather than a one-off submission.
scope_note: This row was oryn-ce's while their lane was open. CEO transferred competition ownership to me when that lane closed, so I researched it rather than leave a 19-day deadline unverified.
recommendation: Add the team-of-4-to-6 and teacher-advisor requirements and the multi-month timeline. For a student seeing this at 19 days out, 'you need to assemble a team and a teacher first' is the single most useful sentence on the record.
unresolved: Whether teams outside the United States may enter — not stated either way.
CORRECTION_2026-08-23: MY DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG AND THE REAL ONE IS MORE INTERESTING. I wrote 'The stored row records none of this'. It does. The row's `description` reads verbatim: 'teams of 4-6 students with a teacher advisor use an online stock market simulator, submit an Investment Policy Statement and a Comprehensive Final Report, and are judged on strategy quality, research depth, and communication rather than portfolio performance.' Flagged by CEO; I verified it in the DB and in the code rather than taking it on trust.
THE_ACTUAL_DEFECT: The fact is recorded but never reaches the layer that decides. `lib/ai/opportunity-context.ts` builds each opportunity line from exactly five things: `recommendation.title`, `recommendation.deadline.date`, `recommendation.why[0]`, the eligibility caveat from `formatEligibilityCaveat`, and the fee caveat from `formatFeeCaveat`. **`description` is not among them.** So the model recommending this row 19 days before its deadline cannot know the student needs to recruit 3-5 classmates and a teacher first.
why_this_strengthens_the_structured_fiel: It sharpens what `self_registration_possible` is FOR. The problem is not always 'nobody wrote it down' — here someone did, in good prose. The problem is that free-text description is expensive and unreliable to push into a prompt, so it is excluded from context by design. A single boolean is cheap and unambiguous, and would survive the trip to the decision layer that the sentence cannot.
how_i_got_it_wrong: Fourth self-correction tonight, same family as the other three: I queried the columns I was auditing (cost, deadline, ages, countries, grades) and concluded from their emptiness, without reading `description`. I inferred absence from the surface I happened to look at.
what_still_stands: The urgency, the 19-day window, the multi-month commitment (deliverables 2026-10-09, 2026-11-06, 2026-12-04; Global Finale 2027-04-29/30), and the fact that a lone student cannot enter. Only the claim about where the gap lives was wrong.

The page differentiates ordering deadlines for schools 'outside of Canada and India', and for at least one contest shows 'Outside North and South America: [contact us]'. So non-Canadian schools clearly can take part, but the arrangement varies by region and in some cases requires contacting CEMC. It is NOT simple open worldwide access, and it is NOT closed either.
eligible_countries: NOT a simple list. Canada and India have standard arrangements; other regions have different deadlines or must contact CEMC. Recorded as conditional rather than filled in.
cost_note: NOT STATED anywhere on the pages retrieved. CEMC contests are known to carry per-student or per-school ordering costs, but no figure is published here, so NULL per the founder's cost rule.
recommendation: Relabel the deadline as a school ordering deadline, add the contest date, record that students cannot self-register, and flag the umbrella problem. A student shown '60 days left' here has no action they can personally take on that date.
unresolved: Per-contest fees.

subject: The stored `deadline` frequently belongs to someone other than the student — three confirmed instances, one more shape
finding: Across the rows I audited, a recurring defect is not a WRONG date but a date whose OWNER is not the student. The number is accurate; the implied action is impossible.

instances.what_it_actually_is: MAA's 'Regular Registration Deadline… Final deadline for new competition managers' — the date a SCHOOL registers as a competition site. MAA states plainly: 'Students and parents do not register directly with the MAA.'
instances.student_reality: The student's action is to persuade their school to register, ideally by the earlier early-bird date of 2026-09-30.

instances.what_it_actually_is: The school's contest ORDERING deadline. Students write on 2026-11-18.
instances.student_reality: Ask a teacher to order the contest.

instances.what_it_actually_is: A genuine registration deadline — but registration requires 'teams of four to six, guided by a teacher from their school as their advisor'.
instances.student_reality: Recruit 3-5 classmates and a teacher, inside 19 days. The date is right; the effort behind it is invisible.

instances.what_it_actually_is: The LAST DAY OF THE CONTEST WINDOW (06-15 April 2027), not an application date at all.
instances.student_reality: There is nothing to apply for — a supervisor registers a team and they sit it during the window.

why_this_is_worse_than_a_missing_date: A missing deadline produces no urgency messaging. A deadline owned by someone else produces CONFIDENT urgency messaging for an action the student cannot perform — 'X days left to apply' for something only their school can do. The student either does nothing and feels the deadline pass, or tries and finds no way in. Both erode trust in the advisor more than silence would.
the_underlying_gap: `deadline` is a single date with no owner and no type. At minimum these are distinct: (a) the student's own submission deadline; (b) an institution's registration or ordering deadline; (c) the date an event takes place; (d) the date a national/qualifying round closes, which is the real first hop for most flagship competitions (see the synthesis, §1).
frequency: Four of the roughly twenty-five rows I examined closely. Given how many rows in the corpus are school-mediated competitions (DECA, HOSA, Science Olympiad, CyberPatriot, FIRST, Congressional App Challenge all have the same institutional shape), the true rate is likely higher.
recommendation: Not a schema proposal from me — but at minimum, research should record WHO the deadline belongs to in prose, and any urgency surface should be cautious about rows whose entry is institution-mediated. The `self_registration_possible` field I added to every record in this lane is a usable proxy: if it is false, the stored date is probably not the student's.
